tagline.text: A five-tier octagonal bell tower in Lingayen's old center

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000~2,000 (Manila round-trip bus and local meals)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: Lingayen Co-Cathedral is the Epiphany (Three Kings) parish church in the Poblacion of Lingayen, the capital of Pangasinan. Its five-tier octagonal bell tower and the Kampana Museum of old bells are the main sights. It pairs well with a walk around Lingayen Gulf and takes 1–2 hours to see.

The formal name is the Co-Cathedral Parish of the Epiphany of Our Lord, formerly Los Tres Reyes, or the Three Kings Church. It stands in the Poblacion (town center) of Lingayen, the capital of Pangasinan, about 200 km from Manila and about 15 km west of the city of Dagupan. It is still a working parish with regular Masses, so visit it as a neighborhood church rather than as a monument.

The history goes back to early Spanish colonial times. Augustinian missionaries brought Catholicism to Lingayen and founded the Three Kings parish, and the Dominicans took it over later. Dates differ by source: Wikipedia lists both 1587 and 1614 for the founding and gives 1616 as the year the parish was formally organized. The present building is variously dated to 1710 or 1712, with a record of a fire and a rebuilding in 1892. This guide does not pin down a single year and reports what the sources say.

In May 1928 the Diocese of Lingayen was created by decree of Pope Pius XI, and this church became its cathedral. In 1963 the diocese was raised to an archdiocese, the seat moved to Dagupan, and Lingayen's church became a co-cathedral. The two cities now share the cathedral role within one archdiocese. Because it is easy to confuse with Dagupan's cathedral, confirm the name Lingayen Co-Cathedral when you choose your destination. The event most tied to this church is the Allied landing in Lingayen Gulf on January 9, 1945: bombing badly damaged the bishop's residence, partly destroyed the church and brought down its centuries-old bells. The July 16, 1990 Luzon earthquake damaged it again, and it was later repaired. A building that has come through war and earthquake still shows the town's ups and downs in its exterior.

What makes this church worth visiting is not its size but the layers of time. An early mission parish founded by Augustinians passed to the Dominicans and then to Filipino priests and Irish Columban missionaries, who are said to have run the parish for about 48 years from 1933. After Spanish rule ended in 1898, Filipino priests took over. Colonial era, war and rebuilding are all in one building, which makes it a good one-hour stop for anyone interested in history, whatever their faith. Lingayen is the administrative center of Pangasinan, so the provincial capitol, city hall, plaza and market sit close together. It is a long trip from Manila for the church alone, but combined with a Dagupan itinerary, the Hundred Islands or a pilgrimage to Manaoag Church it makes a full day. If you are already staying in Pangasinan, it is an easy half-day outing.

The most striking feature is the five-tier octagonal bell tower, said to stand about 45 yards (about 41 m) high. Its pagoda-like, stepped Oriental silhouette is attributed to the influence of Chinese Catholics in the Spanish period. Stand back on the plaza side to get the whole tower in the frame.

The large adobe (brick and lime) nave is described as Neo-Baroque. It was repaired after the 1990 earthquake, but the basic frame is said to follow the old building. The facade decoration and entrance steps are worth a slow look.
The dome over the nave is said to have been built by Fr. Miguel Aparicio, parish priest from 1826 to 1834. Look up to see light coming down through the dome's ceiling and round windows.

blocks.title: Old bells in the Kampana Museum

children.text: The 19th-century bells that fell in the 1945 bombing are known to be displayed in the Kampana (bell) Museum on the church grounds. Opening hours and entry arrangements can change, so check with the parish office before you go.

The main altar and its decorative wall, the nave and the choir loft give the church a calm atmosphere. Religious art in wood and metal is described inside. During Mass, look around quietly so you do not disturb worshippers.
There is a baptismal font said to be the only church piece that survived the war. Ask a staff member or guide where it is.
The Feast of the Three Kings in early January (usually around January 4–6) is said to be the parish's biggest event. The program changes every year, so check the parish announcements.
The plaza in front of the church is where local residents gather, so you can see everyday life. When taking photos, avoid making people's faces the focus, and ask permission during events.

items.title: A 1–2 hour walk around the church
items.subtitle: From the bell tower to the museum

children.text: Arrive early and photograph the whole bell tower from across the plaza. Early hours are quiet and the light is soft.
Climb the front steps and enter the nave. If Mass is under way, stay briefly at the back and leave quietly.
Take your time with the dome, altar and choir loft, and ask where the baptismal font is.
If the Kampana Museum on the grounds is open, look at the old bells. If it is closed, ask at the office.
Walk the Poblacion streets around the church and feel the old-center atmosphere among the market and shops.
Distances inside Lingayen are short, so the town hall plaza and Lingayen beach fit into the same day.

items.title: Extended half-day route
items.subtitle: From the church to Lingayen beach

children.text: After the church visit, have a simple breakfast near the plaza.
Walk around the town hall and the provincial capitol area to see that Lingayen is the administrative center of Pangasinan.
Go to the Lingayen beach side by tricycle or on foot and look at the sea while recalling the 1945 landing.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town, then take a bus to Dagupan or Manila.
The beach can be rough depending on the weather, so follow local advice about swimming.

You can land at Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) or Clark International Airport (CRK) and continue by bus.
Direct links from the airports to Lingayen are not common, so work out your transfer route in advance.
Inside Lingayen Poblacion you can take short tricycle rides or walk.
Fares are negotiated, so state your destination and agree on the price before you board.
The dry season from November to May is best for travel and walking. December–February is especially cool and clear for walking.

Early morning or dawn is the quietest and coolest time to visit the church. Around the Epiphany feast in early January it can be crowded, so choose a weekday morning for a quiet visit or the days around the feast for atmosphere.

Lingayen is small, so you can stay in a small lodging in town or stay in Dagupan, which has more choices, and travel back and forth on the day. This guide does not recommend a specific lodging. Check recent reviews and the location before booking.

You can try Pangasinan local dishes at the market and restaurants in the Poblacion. Dagupan has a wider variety of restaurants, so choose to suit your route. Check the hygiene of street food before eating.

For a day trip, a workable plan is to take an early bus from Manila and leave Lingayen before lunch for Dagupan or Manila. The last Manila-bound bus is listed as running late into the night, but timetables can change, so check before leaving and allow plenty of time.
It is a working parish church, so dress neatly with shoulders and knees covered.
During Mass, do not talk loudly or cross in front, and ask permission before taking photos.
For the best bell tower photo, stand a little back from the plaza so the whole tower fits.
The name is similar to Dagupan's cathedral (the archdiocese's main seat), so search for Lingayen Co-Cathedral in your map app.
The Kampana Museum's opening hours may be irregular, so ask the parish office first.
Combining Lingayen beach and the provincial capitol area on the same day fits a half-day plan well.
In the hot months of March–May, bring water and a hat.
The bus terminal is in Lingayen town, so find out your return options in advance for peace of mind.
It is better to inquire at the parish office during weekday working hours. Check the exact hours locally.
Refrain from sightseeing during Mass and religious events and follow local instructions. Opening and Mass times can change, so check the latest announcements.
Founding and construction years differ by source, so the dates in this guide are for reference.
On holidays and the Epiphany feast there are many visitors and travel can take longer.
In the rainy season (June–November), heavy rain and typhoons can delay travel or cause flooding.
Bus fares and timetables change often, so check the latest information just before departure.
Keep your belongings in front of you in crowded markets and terminals.
The town where the church stands. The beach and the town hall plaza and provincial capitol area are close, within about
10 minutes
of each other.
Said to be the shore where the Allies landed in 1945, close to town. Waves and currents vary with the weather, so check locally whether swimming is possible.
The archdiocese's central city, about
15km
east of Lingayen, where you can continue to Dagupan's other churches and food.
The main island cluster on Pangasinan's western coast, best planned as a separate trip from Lingayen.
Pangasinan's famous pilgrimage church, which you can combine with other church visits in the same region.
